clinicalPearls: A tumour of Schwann-cell (neural) origin composed of large cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm packed with lysosomes
The tongue is the classic site, but it also occurs in the skin, subcutis, breast, gastrointestinal tract, larynx and elsewhere
Diffusely and strongly positive for S100 protein and SOX10, together with markers such as CD68 and inhibin, reflecting its neural differentiation
Small eosinophilic cytoplasmic granules surrounded by clear haloes (pustulo-ovoid bodies of Milian) are a helpful microscopic clue
Overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of squamous epithelium can be mistaken for squamous cell carcinoma on superficial biopsy
The overwhelming majority are benign; a small minority are malignant, defined by features such as necrosis, spindling, high mitotic count, pleomorphism and large size
Named after Abrikossoff, who first described the lesion and proposed a muscle origin later revised to Schwann-cell derivation
reference.pathophysiology: Granular cell tumour arises from Schwann cells, as supported by consistent S100 and SOX10 expression and ultrastructural features. The characteristic granular cytoplasm reflects the accumulation of autophagic lysosomes rather than true myoblastic differentiation, correcting the original myoblastoma concept. A proportion of cases carry loss-of-function alterations in genes encoding endosomal or lysosomal regulators, consistent with the lysosome-rich phenotype. Most tumours grow slowly and behave in a benign fashion, with only rare examples showing the atypical or malignant features that predict aggressive behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Squamous cell carcinoma, when pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is prominent
Rhabdomyoma and other granular or oncocytic tumours
Melanoma with granular or oncocytic change
additionalInvestigations: Immunohistochemistry for S100 and SOX10 to confirm neural (Schwann-cell) differentiation
Adjunctive markers such as CD68, inhibin, calretinin and TFE3 as needed
Deep or repeat biopsy when superficial sampling shows only reactive epithelial hyperplasia
Assessment of atypical histological features to gauge malignant potential
Imaging to define lesion extent and detect multifocal disease at unusual sites
Complete excision specimen review to assess margins and exclude malignancy
redFlags: Rapid growth, large size or ulceration suggesting the malignant variant
Histological atypia with necrosis, spindling, prominent nucleoli or increased mitoses
Regional lymph node or distant metastasis
Multiple lesions or visceral involvement requiring broader evaluation
reference.prognosis: Benign granular cell tumours are cured by complete local excision, with recurrence mainly related to incomplete removal; the rare malignant variant can metastasise to lymph nodes, lung and bone and carries a substantially worse outlook, so recognition of atypical features and adequate resection are important.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing squamous cell carcinoma because of overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia on a shallow biopsy
Mistaking the granular cytoplasm for a histiocytic or xanthomatous process
Failing to sample deeply enough to reach the diagnostic granular cells
Assuming all lesions are benign and not assessing for malignant histological criteria
Overlooking multifocal disease at less typical anatomical sites
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Head and Neck Tumours
management: Complete local surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay and is usually curative for the benign tumour
Confirm the diagnosis histologically with S100 and SOX10 immunohistochemistry, using adjuncts such as CD68 and inhibin where needed
Take a deep or repeat biopsy when superficial sampling shows only pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, to avoid overcalling squamous cell carcinoma
Assess atypical histological features (necrosis, spindling, high mitotic count, pleomorphism, large size) to gauge malignant potential
For the rare malignant variant, perform wide excision with regional lymph node assessment, as it responds poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy
Image to define lesion extent and detect multifocal disease at unusual sites
Follow up for local recurrence, which chiefly reflects incomplete removal, and refer malignant or atypical cases to a soft tissue oncology multidisciplinary team
